evidence_spans: Inks for 3D printing were prepared by mixing and suspending five powders – Ti (mass: 2.96 g, purity: ≥99%, powder size: <25 µm, supplier: AP&C), ZrH 2 (5.66 g, 99%, 2 µm, US Research Nanomaterials, Inc), HfH 2 (10.95 g, >99.9%, 1–10 µm, NANOCHEMAZONE), Nb (5.75 g, 99.8%, 1–5 µm, Thermo Scientific), TaH 0.5 (11.01 g, 99.9%, 2 µm, Thermo Scientific) powders – in dichloromethane (40 mL, DCM, Sigma–Aldrich), with the following additions: i) polystyrene (1.67 g, PS, Mw = 350 k, Sigma–Aldrich) as binder, ii) dibutyl phthalate (0.4 g, DBP, Sigma–Aldrich) as plasticizer, iii) ethylene glycol butyl ether (2.4 g, EGBE, Sigma–Aldrich) as surfactant.

The Ti and Nb powder are each purposely slightly over‐stoichiometric (as 20.2 at.%) in the powder blend, to compensate for the possible loss during ball milling (as ductile powders often stick to the balls).
Roller milling was carried out in high‐density polyethylene (HDPE, 120 mL) bottle for 12 h to mix the full wet ink with zirconia balls (ball to powder ratio: 1:1).
The viscosity of the inks was adjusted by DCM evaporation at 50 °C to get a printable ink (the rheological properties of the PS‐DBP‐DCM ink system have been studied in detail in Ref. [ [64] ]).
Extrusion printing was performed with a 3D‐Bioplotter (EnvisionTEC, Germany) with conical 410 µm plastic nozzles (Nordson EFD).
The 9 × 9 × 9 mm 3 lattices were printed with a layer height of 320 µm, a horizontal spacing of 0.8 mm, and a layer rotation angle of 90°.
After drying, these ink‐cast ingots were cut with a razor blade into cuboids (approximate size: (7‐13) × (5‐7) × 5 mm 3 ) which were used to explore the sintering and siliconizing processes.
The formation of HfC, caused by carbon contamination during debinding, is anticipated, given that HfC is more stable than the carbide of Zr, Ta, Nb, and Ti, and thus forms preferentially.
Additive manufacturing of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr is implemented by extruding inks containing hydride powders, de‐binding under H 2 , and sintering under vacuum.

research_thread.sample_lineage: Powder hydrides -> De-bound ink -> Printed lattice/cuboid -> Sintered (1400°C, 15min-18h) -> Homogenized (1500°C) or Coated
research_thread.intervention: Variable sintering time (15 min - 18 h), Ti sponges as oxygen getter, Silicide coating via pack cementation.
research_thread.baseline: Uncoated sintered samples; bulk cylinders for intrinsic property comparison.
research_thread.conditions: Vacuum (<3e-6 torr), Hydrogen (debinding), Argon (coating), 1400-1500 °C thermal steps.
research_thread.structure: Initially printed green parts with binder; transitions to near fully dense polycrystalline BCC/HCP (quenched to single BCC) microstructure.
research_thread.outcome: High-temperature mechanical properties (yield strength, energy absorption) and improved oxidation resistance via silicide coating (parabolic rate constant reduction).
research_thread.mechanism: Sequential decomposition of hydrides to form alloy; Ti getter prevents oxidation during sintering; Silicide coating forms protective SiO2 scale.

Second, sintering was performed at 1400 °C, for times spanning between 15 min and 18 h, in a vacuum tube furnace with an initial vacuum level of < 3 × 10 −6 torr.
A zirconium foil was used to cover the crucible containing the samples and titanium sponges were placed in the crucible to act as an oxygen getter during sintering.

research_thread.scientific_problem: Deciphering the kinetic sequence of hydride decomposition in HfNbTaTiZr powder blends to optimize the formation of a single-phase, high-purity alloy during rapid sintering.
research_thread.sample_lineage: Hydrided ink (730°C, 2h) -> In situ XRD heating (100-1000°C) -> Sintered bulk/lattice (1400°C).
research_thread.intervention: In situ XRD monitoring of dehydrogenation; Sequential heating from 100 to 1000 °C under vacuum.
research_thread.baseline: Standard powder blend without in situ monitoring (implied), or comparing decomposition rates of different hydrides.
research_thread.conditions: Vacuum (≈10^-3 torr), Mo source, 5 °C steps, 120 s exposure.
research_thread.structure: Sequential disappearance of hydride phases (TaH0.5, NbH, TiH2, HfH2, ZrH2) and appearance of metallic phases (BCC, HCP).
research_thread.outcome: Revealed sequential decomposition order (Ta/Nb -> Ti/Hf -> Zr) and identification of HfC formation in sintered samples.
research_thread.mechanism: Thermal decomposition of metal hydrides driven by temperature and vacuum, followed by solid-state diffusion to form the HEA.
research_thread.hypothesis_value: The sequential nature of hydride decomposition dictates the sintering kinetics; the slow dehydrogenation of ZrH2 is the likely bottleneck for achieving full homogenization in rapid sintering protocols.
alternative_explanations: HfC formation is due to binder decomposition products reacting with Hf rather than incomplete hydride dehydrogenation.
The observed sequence might be an artifact of the heating rate or detector sensitivity.
null_or_negative_results: None explicitly, but the persistence of HfC is a negative outcome for purity.
missing_information: Quantitative rate constants for each hydride decomposition step.
